title: Flexible working, reasonable adjustments and barriers to disabled employment
label: 21 October 2026 · Flexible work and disability
summary: Witnesses from the Business Disability Forum and the Trades Union Congress told the committee that while many employers offer flexible working and reasonable adjustments, there are persistent delays, inconsistent practice, limited enforcement, and cultural stigma that keep disabled people out of work or stuck in worse roles. They urged clearer guidance, faster and better-resourced Access to Work support, stronger legal rights (including advertising flexibility and a default right to flexible work), better employer accountability than the current Disability Confident scheme, and practical workplace measures such as adjustment passports and equality reps.

chapters.title: Where employers reach the limits of flexibility
chapters.takeaway: Large employers say they often provide many adjustments but hit organisational limits that need clearer rules and planning.

turns.speaker: Rachel Taylor
turns.text: Angela, you said some businesses have reached the limit of what they can offer in flexibility. Which businesses are you talking about?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: BDF mostly works with very large employers—tens of thousands of staff. They tell us they've introduced lots of adjustments, redeployments and flexible roles, but eventually those changes reshape where staff sit in the business and cause organisational strain.

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: This is most obvious where there are many front-line roles—healthcare, police, retail—and back-office roles. Flexible working under employment law can be seen as permanent, while reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act are about what the person needs now.

turns.speaker: Rachel Taylor
turns.text: Could employers organise roles and retrain people to be more inclusive?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Yes, but retraining takes time and resource. Smaller employers especially struggle to upskill staff so there are suitable vacancies for redeployment when someone's role becomes unsuitable.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: From unions' roundtables, employers sometimes don't consult enough or think creatively. For example, they reject part-time requests without checking job sharing; they often give vague reasons under the 'eight business reasons' and don't show evidence for refusals.

chapters.title: Guidance, legislation and what should be mandatory
chapters.takeaway: Both witnesses want clearer rules and some legal changes: better guidance, advertising of flexibility, and possibly a default right to flexible work.

turns.speaker: Rachel Taylor
turns.text: Should Government use guidance or law to encourage flexible working?

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Guidance helps, but the TUC wants legal change. Voluntary approaches often fail—gender pay gap reporting improved only once made mandatory. Stronger law is needed for less-unionised sectors.

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Employers say they want to consider the sustainability of a flexible arrangement—whether it conflicts with future business plans—so they want clarity in the ERA about longer-term reasonableness.

turns.speaker: Rachel Taylor
turns.text: Would sector- and role-specific guidance help employers offer flexible working more widely?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Yes, because large employers have many different roles. For some roles flexibility focuses on output; for others operational requirements rule it out. Employers could audit which roles are full-time only and which can flex.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: The April 2024 changes barely shifted access to good-quality flexible working. We support an advertising duty to list flexible options in job adverts and a default right to flexibility, unless an employer can objectively justify refusal.

turns.speaker: Rachel Taylor
turns.text: Any evidence that advertising flexibility works?

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Yes. Timewise found around 30% of jobs include flexible options currently. Zurich advertised flexibility on all roles and saw a 66% rise in applications and more part-time hires; HR managers say adding flexibility to adverts would be easy.

chapters.title: Delays and gaps in reasonable adjustments and Access to Work
chapters.takeaway: Many disabled people wait months for adjustments; Access to Work is slow, under-reaches workers, and enforcement is weak.

turns.speaker: Nadia Whittome
turns.text: TUC research shows most disabled workers needing adjustments don't get them fully. Why?

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Barriers include fear of rejection—six in 10 don't ask—long waits, incorrect refusals and poor treatment. In our survey, 55% who requested adjustments got only some or none; 19% were given no reason for refusal.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Access to Work is part of the problem: the NAO found 40% of funded support should have been supplied by employers, and Access to Work reaches only about 1% of disabled workers despite doubling spending.

turns.speaker: Nadia Whittome
turns.text: Should employers have a tight deadline to respond to adjustment requests—say two weeks?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Faster is good, but two weeks isn't always realistic. The decision can be quick, but procuring support—like a job coach or specialist kit—and waiting for Access to Work can take months. We need pragmatic timeframes and faster Access to Work.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: One improvement would be in-principle indicative awards from Access to Work so employers can act quickly while formal funding is confirmed. The Disability Employment Charter suggests a two-week target, but it needs practical roll-out plans.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: We also need stronger EHRC enforcement: its budget and capacity have fallen sharply since 2007 and it lacks resources for targeted enforcement of employers who flout adjustment duties.

chapters.title: Workplace practices that help: passports, reps and inclusive job design
chapters.takeaway: Practical workplace tools—adjustment passports, equality reps, accessible adverts and inclusive procurement—make adjustments stick and reduce repeat requests.

turns.speaker: Richard Quigley
turns.text: Supported internships seem effective; what encourages employers to use them?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Employers find the schemes are often confusing: many programme names and different local arrangements. We need simple, business-friendly explanations so supported internships are seen as mainstream recruitment routes, not niche projects.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Practical steps include reasonable adjustment passports so a worker's needs travel with them, and stronger workplace equality reps who help negotiate and monitor practice.

turns.speaker: Kevin McKenna
turns.text: Should all jobs be advertised flexible-by-default—then employers must explain the small set that can't be?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: It depends what 'flexible' means. Job descriptions are crucial because they define how someone is measured. For very small teams or time-critical roles there are real limits, so we need sensible detail in job descriptions, not just adverts.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: The TUC wants flexibility to be the norm and adverts to reflect that; we also back collective agreements and union-negotiated approaches that reduce sporadic individual requests.

chapters.title: Mandates, office return policies and employer accountability
chapters.takeaway: Blanket office-return mandates can harm disabled workers; better equality impact assessments, union involvement and accountability schemes are needed.

turns.speaker: Richard Quigley
turns.text: What is the evidence for broad return-to-office mandates?

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Many mandates come from senior leaders and lack evidence they improve collaboration or productivity. Studies show disabled workers strongly prefer remote or hybrid options—around 65% said they wanted remote work—and mandates have worsened outcomes for many disabled staff.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: For instance, some surveys found disabled respondents reporting worse productivity and work–life balance under mandates compared to non-disabled colleagues.

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Mandates aren't always wrong, but they mustn't become a way to exclude disabled staff. Leaders sometimes want people together for cultural reasons, which can be valuable, but employers should do equality impact assessments and consider alternatives.

turns.speaker: Alex Brewer
turns.text: Only 6% of people with a learning disability are employed. What would increase that?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Employers fear getting it wrong and worry about reputational risk. Better promotion of local supported work programmes, accessible adverts and simpler procurement choices would help employers start small and scale up.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Also change insecure work rules so more workers have employee status and access to flexible-working rights; unions support co-design and mandatory protections alongside employer guidance.

turns.speaker: Alex Brewer
turns.text: How should we replace or reform Disability Confident?

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Disabled workers say Disability Confident has had limited impact and can be a marketing tool. We want independent verification, co-design with disabled people and unions, and measurable thresholds—Germany's quota and levy model was given as an example.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any closing practical suggestions?

turns.speaker: Angela Matthews
turns.text: Practical things: audit which roles can flex, make job descriptions clearer, speed up Access to Work, use health and safety law alongside equality law, and fund better EHRC enforcement.

turns.speaker: Daisy Goodall
turns.text: Plus: advertise flexible options in vacancies, push for a default right to flexible work, support adjustment passports and equality reps, and insist on independent verification for employer accreditation schemes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both — those are very helpful and practical recommendations. Please follow up with any material you think would assist the inquiry.
